subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF CONTRACT WITH COMPUTING DEVICES IN CONNECTION WITH SAMSON PROJECT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 with respect to the matter of Computing Devices of Canada and the cancellation of the Samson contract and their participation in it. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald):
That a thorough investigation be undertaken by the Department of Supply and Services as to the fairness in the evaluation of the product of CDC in light of the conditions of unprecedented security that are the cause of the delays and were beyond the control of the company by reason of, first, lack of U.S. security information as promised; second, lack of Canadian government security information as promised; and third, the fact that this was therefore the first Canadian company to undertake the development and establishment of tempest technology.
Further, that pending the investigation, the Crown reinstate the contract on the basis that the company can meet the delivery requirement of September 1976 for the prearranged testing and implementation of the system.

speechtext:
Before commencing the question period I know all hon. members of the House would want to join with me in taking just a moment to mark the significance
12176

of this occasion in celebration of an anniversary of an event which took place on March 26, 1940, some 36 years ago. I refer, of course, to the first of an unbroken succession of elections to the House of Commons of the Right Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MEMBER FOR PRINCE ALBERT ON THIRTY-SIXTH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION AS MEMBER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MEMBER FOR PRINCE ALBERT ON THIRTY-SIXTH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION AS MEMBER
speechtext:
The incidence of an unbroken succession of elections to this House is a remarkable occurrence, appreciated perhaps no more clearly than by the other members of this chamber. In addition to the success the right hon. member has enjoyed during that time at the hands of the electors and the honours which have been heaped upon him by Canadians in every walk of life as well as from every corner of the country, perhaps the highest honour the Canadian citizenry can pay to any one of us is to elect a person to be Prime Minister and first citizen of our country, which is at the pinnacle of those great honours and distinctions.
However, to add to that achievement, and as a recognition which I think all of us share with immense pride, the right hon. gentleman will leave Canada tomorrow for the United Kingdom where he will be received by Her Majesty the Queen and recognized as a Companion of Honour, a recognition which is shared by only 65 members of the Commonwealth, and perhaps most significantly the motto of which is, "in action faithful, in honour clear". It is in that expression of the record of service of the right hon. gentleman that all of us, and I am sure all Canadians, share with great pride and wish him well on that journey, in receiving that honour, and in continued devotion and work on behalf of this country.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-89, to amend the Anti-Inflation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is my first opportunity to speak on second reading of this bill. I hope that Your Honour will hear me out, because I am raising a point of order. It is a rather detailed point of order for which I ask Your Honour's indulgence for about five minutes so that I can put it before you. I am satisfied that Your Honour will have to reserve opinion on it, but here it is. It comes back, basically, to the point I have raised time and time again with regard to bills, and that is that some bills go beyond any recommendation made. In this instance, to come down to a nub, there is in this bill, as there was in Bill C-73 which Bill C-89 attempts to amend, provision, under sections 20 and following in Bill C-73 and in clause 6 of this particular bill, for the government of Canada to enter into an agreement with the provinces with respect to the enforcement of the guidelines and all the consequent provisions.
On January 9, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) filed a model agreement and in paragraph 9 of that model agreement there are the following words:
"Payments to the province". Canada hereby agrees, with respect to the aggregate amount paid to Her Majesty in right of Canada pursuant to any order made by the national administrator under sections 20 and 22 of the federal act-
That is now chapter 75 of the statutes of 1974-75-76.
-against a person in the provincial public sector, to pay to the province an amount equal to such part of that amount as may be determined on the basis of a formula to be agreed upon between Canada and the province.
That provision was incorporated as paragraph 9 in an agreement made January 13, 1976, between the government of Canada and the province of Ontario. Basically, there is a situation where revenues resulting from orders of the administrator are paid into the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. Then there is an agreement by the minister, with the approval of the governor in council, to pay moneys out of the consolidated revenue fund to the province, calculated on a proportion of an amount paid into the fund. But under our constitutional and procedural requirements there are two conditions which apply to such payment out of the consolidated revenue fund. First, His Excellency the Governor General must recommend the payment for that purpose in his message to this House. Second, the legislation based upon the message must authorize the payment. We already have had one amendment to the recommendation preceding Bill C-73, and neither the original recommendation nor the amended recommendation says anything about payment of such funds to
Anti-Inflation Act
the provinces. The recommendation is limited to administrative expenses.
Bill C-89, which amends the appropriate clauses of Bill C-73 with regard to these agreements, has no recommendation. I should like to refer Your Honour to clause 6, subclauses (1) (2) and (3) of Bill C-89, and it is my submission that these subclauses, relating directly to payments to Her Majesty in the right of Canada, put this constitutional and procedural defect right at issue. I will summarize briefly. It is a combination of Bill C-73, which has no provision for payment of funds from Canada to the provinces, and the model agreement tabled by the minister and entered into by some minister, on the part of the government of Canada, with the province of Ontario-and, strangely enough, to show that the government is conscious of this fact, in the agreement with the province of Quebec there is no mention of payments from the government of Canada to the province of Quebec, because Quebec does its own administering.
In the case of New Brunswick, the money the administrator directed that the Irving Paper Company pay to the government of Canada is subject to an agreement and is shared between the government of Canada and the government of the province in question. However, there is no authority for that sharing in any recommendation or in Bill C-73, which we have passed, and there was no model agreement. The model agreement followed the passage of Bill C-73 and, as I say, Bill C-89, clause 6, refers directly to these agreements and to the payments thereunder. Since there is no recommendation, it is my view that the bill as prepared is defective, imperfect and requires an amendment by the bringing in of an appropriate recommendation that this House will authorize the payment or the sharing of these moneys paid under the order of the administrator with a province.
I am not going to hold up the legislation, but in my submission this will have to be done. That is my submission to Your Honour for this purpose at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a few words on this bill and to add my comments to what I think is a very important problem. There is a growing number of people and organizations in Canada who are joining in the chorus that wage and price controls are essentially wrong, and that they should be removed as soon as possible before too much harm is done for the future. Last Monday morning, the cabinet listened to the highly-selective and well-prepared brief of the Canadian Labour Congress which feels that the bill deals unfairly with organized labour. Page 9 of that brief gives an indication of what they think:
Your government's program was supposed to be equitable. Canadians were told that the same degree of sacrifice would be required from all sectors of the community. The legislation and the regulations have made a mockery of this principle for we fail to find adequate controls on dividends, interest rates, professional fees and land speculators. The removal of the special levy on export profits is a clear demonstration that workers in these industries will not benefit from the profits which they worked to produce. Neither is there any guarantee that these profits will be reinvested in Canada to create badly needed jobs. The inequities are becoming clearer with the passage of each day.
While I do not agree that things are as bad for organized labour as this brief states, I do think the inequities are there. Certainly, when the leaders for large numbers of well-organized unions make presentations, we cannot dismiss them and the anti-inflation program must be looked at carefully. The congress listed injustices that they feel were perpetrated in this country by the Anti-Inflation Board. I think it is significant that they have carried out their threat to withdraw from the Canada Labour Relations Council, amongst other bodies. When I consider how the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) for a long time was seeking ways to reduce labour strikes and increase consultation between government, labour and business, I am concerned about this withdrawal. Now we are back to square one as far as concerns the government's attempts to bring peace to labour-management problems in this country. Other voices are being heard. Last Monday, the Ottawa Journal reported that the Canadian Economic Policy Committee of the C. D. Howe Institute had this to say:
Forecasts indicating little if any improvement in the rate of inflation, a further rise in unemployment and only modest gains in over-all productivity do not constitute an outlook for the Canadian economy in 1976 that can be viewed with equanimity.
They stand in sharp contrast to the performance expected in a number of other major industrial economies, particularly the United States economy where the need for greater discipline in its policies was recognized sooner and implemented faster than in Canada.
I think it is important to note that the government has backed off the export tax. In effect, what they have said is that we will now have a two-price system for Canadian
March 26, 1976

goods-what the company can get in Canada, and what they can get in the export market. Almost certainly, the export market price will be higher, which means that shortages will develop if the controls are allowed to continue. That raises the possibility of an attempt by the government to direct into the domestic market a portion of the production of the various companies.
The C.D. Howe Institute went on to say that at present the government has an opportunity to implement sound economic policies. They recommended that the growth of money supply be limited to 10 per cent, and that government spending be restrained while import barriers and government subsidies are reduced. They also urged the government to remove its wage and price controls at the earliest possible date, and said that in their view, any long continuance of the controls increases the risk that government will delay the adoption of a sound package of basic economic measures. The real crisis lies in inadequate leadership and a failure to make full use of the market system, they claim.
The government is faced with the possibility of keeping controls on too long and using them as a means of dealing with inflation rather than getting the economy into shape. We will get the worst of both worlds. As has been pointed out many times, during the election campaign of 1974 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that wage and price controls did not work and he would not use them. The Prime Minister is quoted as having stated on February 28, 1974:
Income controls risk hurting the small and the poor more than they do the big and the rich; and while that may be of minor concern to the more conservative governments and political parties, it is of great and fundamental concern to this government.
The Canadian Labour Congress brief aptly pointed out that the government had degraded the political process in Canada and spread cynicism in the public about government and politics in general. This turnabout by the Prime Minister stands as one of the greatest political turnabouts in the history of Canadian politics. Also, in this bill the government indicates that it is merely tinkering with the process of the functioning of the Anti-Inflation Board without making it in reality any more effective than it was before. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) put it very succinctly when he said that Canada and Canadians are living through an economic experiment. Even with all the wage and price controls being tried in other countries with economies somewhat similar to Canada, such as the United Kingdom and the United States, controls were shown up to be only superficial in attempting to cope with inflation. Speaking on November 14, 1975, on the New Democratic Party motion, I had this to say:
What about inflation? The latest consumer index showing inflation at just over 10 per cent does not come into the category of "good tidings of great joy" but neither is it runaway inflation. It is down from last year. The declining rates of inflation in wholesale prices and commodity prices can be expected to work their way down through the grocery shelves. For instance, the wholesale price index for September announced this week was 6.1 per cent up over a year earlier and the price of raw and partially finished goods was up only 2.5 per cent in the year. The enormous and bumper crops in the United States of grain have pushed down the basic price of corn, wheat, oil seeds so that at the present price the farmer is producing the level of return of 1972 before the devaluation of the American dollar.
Anti-Inflation Act
I think this indicates that the stage was set long before the anti-inflation bill was brought in to have a reduction in the price of many goods. We were saying that Canadian wage settlements were being reduced. I think we have to remember that with the devaluation of the American dollar by 40 per cent two years ago, much of the increase in wages can be attributed to the readjustment that this would inevitably bring. In the third quarter of last year, before the government decided on wage and price controls, wage settlements in the commercial industry averaged only 13 per cent over the life of the contract. This is certainly not far behind the 12 per cent allowed under the guidelines for workers who have fallen behind because of inflation.
The government can point out that the consumer price index, whatever its value as an index of inflation, has dropped considerably. The rate of increase of the money stock has slowed, and the average rate of increase in major wage settlements improved in the fourth quarter of 1975. This might indicate that these key economic indicators have all shown substantial improvement, but the link between the improvement and the controls is almost nonexistent. The consumer price index is down because of declines since October in the price of beef, pork, poultry, fresh fruit, cereal and bakery products, fats, oils, and airline fares. Of all these, only air fares come under the Anti-Inflation Board's purview. Further, the board has only just begun monitoring price and profit margins in a formal way.
On January 28, the board took its first formal step requiring 6,500 companies to provide information by February 27 on prices, profit margins, dividends and compensation. In March, the net was extended to cover a further 9,500 companies in construction, shipping and other industries where small firms conduct joint bargaining with their employees. It will probably take a considerable time for the true effects of the guidelines on prices to become apparent, although the board relatively soon may identify and publicly punish firms which contravene the guidelines.
Although some of the moderation in wage rates during the fourth quarter is attributable to the operation of the guidelines, I am of the opinion that most of the decline would have taken place in any case. The guidelines do not apply to settlements below 10 per cent, or 12 per cent in special cases. In cases where the board has intervened, many of the settlements allowed were only marginally below the previously negotiated increases. Since its first decision of November 27, the board has ruled only on about 160 settlements: another 340 await approval. Of the 160 settlements dealt with, 26 were rolled back an average of 3.9 per cent. The average first-year increase allowed in these settlements was 16.2 per cent. The average wage increase in all approved settlements so far has equalled about 14 per cent.
Wage settlements in this period have moderated, primarily because of high unemployment, falling inflation rates and mounting employer resistance to high claims. This could have been forecast last March, long before the controls were initiated. The controls program very likely will have little effect on the average rate of increase in

March 26, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
wage settlements as the months go by. The controls program will have some effect, but only through supervision of price increases which in any event would have come about through stable or rising profit margins in current economic expansion. In other words, in the long run, the board may depress allowable profits and there will be considerable trouble down the road.
The deliberate sacrifice of profit margins cannot be allowed to continue for long without causing undesirable distortions in the economy. A restraining monetary policy, together with a move away from net stimulus in fiscal policy, is now evident. Together, these policies will be responsible in large part for preventing a price explosion when the controls are softened or lifted. The government will not find it easy to manage the period of transition. There will be a tendency for prices to rise when the controls are lifted. Some companies are not raising prices at present because they are not sure exactly what the guidelines allow. Most people want to remain within the guidelines; few want to break the law. Once people know how much extra they can charge under the anti-inflation guidelines, they will charge as much as they can. I am afraid that the minimum increase will be the maximum allowed under the guidelines.
In summary, at this stage it seems as if the country will meet the government's inflation targets for 1976 and 1977, December to December increases in the consumer price index of 8 per cent and 6 per cent respectively. To date, the effect of the controls program has probably been minimal, but its effects will cumulatively be more important as time goes on. It will be necessary for fiscal and monetary policies to be sufficiently restraining during and after the controls period to make certain that no price explosion occurs when the distortions caused by controls are worked out in freer bargaining after the program's end.
It is increasingly evident that the problems of our controls are just beginning. Mr. Pepin, head of the Anti-Inflation Board, has warned that prices will rise as soon as business people realize what they are entitled to charge under the plan. Actually, the controls program indexes inflation at around 10 per cent. It is quite likely that inflation will rise at this rate and the program will make things worse rather than better. The period of control obviously will be extremely unsettling. The longer decontrols stay on, the worse the period of decontrol will be, and the stronger will be the desire of certain groups-perhaps the government included-to see permanent controls remain. These could further distort the economy. Undoubtedly the government has made poor decisions in the past few years; the results of these are going to show up. In our major markets, the United States in particular, there has been a greater tendency to allow market forces to make their way. These economies will be the stronger for it.
I find one aspect of this bill unsettling, namely, the attempt to bring into the ambit of the AIB many small companies which have hitherto been exempt, especially construction companies. There is no obvious reason for this. There has been no public demand for it and no evidence that these people were upsetting the balance which the controls were designed to achieve. This aspect of the bill seems to be based solely on a recommendation of the former prices and incomes commission. The worthy

chairman of that commission advanced no reasons for his recommendation. Frankly, I think it is a mistake to do this. After all, it is in direct conflict with the Prime Minister's theory of government, the Galbraithian theory, which holds that small firms cannot be monopolies and cannot create distortions in the marketplace because they are too small. In other words, small companies respond to the discipline of the marketplace and competition holds down undue gains. Perhaps the moral is that once you start controlling, you must control everything.
May I now deal with the Anti-Inflation Board's decision relating to bilingual civil servants. The Anti-Inflation Board has ruled that bilingualism bonuses for civil servants are not compensation increases subject to wage and salary guidelines. According to newspaper reports, these will cost the federal government $60 million or more in the next year or two. It has been argued that provision was made for such compensation before the controls program was instituted.
I point out that the board did not hesitate to criticize the government's wage settlement with the postal workers. It seems to me that it ought to have rolled back the proposed bilingual increases. Of course, it is up to the government to decide if such roll-back is fair, if the extra $60 million should be paid under government policy. If the government were to so decide, well and good. I submit that the government was responsible for making a decision with regard to bilingual employees, not the Anti-Inflation Board. I raise this matter since it is apparent that we are operating under a double standard. The Anti-Inflation Board has favoured public employees over private employees. If it is to function effectively, it must be objective. It is the government's responsibility to decide what policies it wishes to implement with respect to the bilingual program, or what it wants to pay postal workers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am especially pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-89, an act to amend the Anti-Inflation Act, because I did not participate in the debate on the original bill, C-73, passed on December 3 last. Although I attended nearly every meeting of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs during the consideration of the original bill and was prepared to contribute to the debate, I thought it was better to defer to my colleagues on this side of the House who had not been able to put their views on record before the government imposed closure once more.
I was greatly surprised, however, that less than four months after the passage of Bill C-73 the government proposed an amending bill. Already, through the regulations, the minister had effected certain changes; for example, dividends for small companies, although the public companies still have their dividends frozen. Under the original rules, one area of inequity was that dealing with dividends. Recognizing the effects of inflation, wages were to be allowed to increase 8, 10 or 12 per cent in certain circumstances. However, dividends were frozen at the levels paid in 1974 or those declared in 1975. Furthermore, this not only applied to the largest companies, but to all companies, including small businesses which rely on their dividend policy as part of their remuneration plan. Excep-
March 26, 1976

tions, the minister says, were to be allowed if they could get through the Anti-Inflation Board line-up of cases of corporations needing higher dividends to attract new capital or those for which the base rate was unusually low. It is not hard to imagine the effect this policy had on investors. Many of them probably went to United States markets in the meantime.
The government attack apparently ignored the fact that many retired Canadians rely to a greater or lesser degree on dividend income. These thrifty Canadians who are now to have their dividend income frozen are the very ones the government should be encouraging so that more and more Canadians will want to save and invest instead of spending every last nickel today.
The minister was unable to explain, during the committee hearings, how the pensioner was to get along with a frozen income at the same time that wages were to be allowed to rise. You may say, yes, but government pensions are indexed and that will take care of the pensioner. Although most government pensions are indexed, the private schemes with which they are often co-ordinated usually offset the government increase with a reduction of the private portion, so that the number of dollars paid remains constant. This, of course, works a great hardship on pensioners in these days of high inflation rates.
The government has also overlooked the plight of the ordinary pension funds, the mutual funds and insurance companies. These companies invest the hard-earned savings of low and middle income Canadians, giving nearly every working Canadian some kind of interest in dividends. Every little guy who has an insurance policy, pension plan or any kind of savings has an interest in the dividends of Canadian corporations. But look at the financial attacks being made on the ordinary pension fund today. For one thing, pensioners are living longer and therefore are making greater demands than were predicted when these funds were set up. Of course, the drop in value of the dollar means that more demands are being made on pension funds for increased pensions. In the period since 1965, wages have gone up 126 per cent, but dividends have gone up only 32 per cent, further curtailing the pension funds and stimulating demand for higher pensions. Falling markets have in many cases resulted in capital losses for these pension funds. The government proposes to continue this freeze on dividends. Many pension funds are having great difficulty remaining actuarially sound as a result of all these forces. I suspect that more serious trouble will lie ahead.
I often refer, in my remarks, to the little guy, the little investor and the widows and orphans who have substantial interests in Canadian corporations. Others, particularly those to my left, make frequent reference, with scorn, to the corporate welfare bums. It is significant to see how far into the Canadian corporate structure the individual shareholder has penetrated. To give an example, I point to the International Nickel Company of Canada Limited, which has 55,000 registered shareholders in Canada. Undoubtedly, there are many more who are beneficial owners through trusts and other vehicles. This 55,000 is three times the total number of hourly workers employed by the International Nickel Company of Canada, Limited. These 55,000 shareholders have had their dividends frozen,
Anti-Inflation Act
while the wages of one-third that number of hourly workers are allowed to rise 8, 10 or 12 per cent in certain cases.
Before government members say to me that we in the official opposition proposed this kind of a plan, I wish to refer to one or two statements that have been made by government people and others. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), in the House on October 17, 1975, denied that there was any relationship between his plan and our plan. He said:
As I anticipated, the leader of the opposition could not resist the temptation to characterize the program now being put forward by the government as a vindication of the mandatory, comprehensive prices and incomes control program he advocated during the last election campaign and for 15 months before that. It is, of course, nothing of the kind.
I wish to refer as follows to the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) given to the accountability session of the Liberal party in Ottawa on November 9 last year:
And we are not the Tories, for instance, who say in one breath that we are stealing their program against inflation and who say in the next, it can't work because we did not follow their program on inflation. We are not following their program on inflation.
During the committee hearings there was another reference that tended to show there was no similarity between the programs. I wish to refer to a question I directed to Mr. Hughes, the executor director of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I asked:
Do you see any major differences between this program and the program that was proposed by the Progressive Conservative Party in 1974?
Mr. Hughes replied:
Yes, sir.
He went on to explain the differences that he saw.

I do not believe there was any mention of it, Mr. Speaker. Long before this bill was introduced certain changes were announced by the minister. The changes were to include, as I remember, 41,000 new companies or firms that would be covered by the guidelines. They were to include all firms in the construction, trucking, grain handling, longshoring and shipping industries. Just last week the minister also said he was considering including the insurance industry in the control program.
Originally, the bill was only to apply to large companies. A number of organizations appeared before the committee.

Anti-Inflation Act
At that time the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, which claims a membership of 4,500 companies and 9,000 individual members, stated that only 350 of their 4,500 companies would be covered and that none of their individual members would be covered. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce estimated that of its 125,000 members in Canada, some 1,500 would be covered-just over 1 per cent.
Then we heard from the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen that probably none of its 30,000 members would be covered. The Canadian Construction Association made an estimate that close to 10 per cent of the firms engaged in the construction industry would be made subject to the guidelines. In the labour sector, the CLC indicated that although the proportion in their case would be higher, less than half their members would be covered by the guidelines. It is interesting to note that the Employers' Council of British Columbia, a noted organization in the field, was refused the opportunity to appear before the standing committee to present its views and ideas.
Then, of course, before the amending bill was presented we were able to hear the Prime Minister's year-end address delivered only a few weeks after the passage of the original bill. Even though the opposition had mounted a vigorous attack on the length of the control period, the Prime Minister indicated in his address that our society was not working to his satisfaction and that we might be faced with a permanent variety of controls. Last week, after all this, the minister took more than 30 minutes to explain the amendments to the three-months' old bill, C-73. The most significant, he told us, were those related to the appeals system. He also proposed the broadening of the right to appeal, and changes in the rules regarding increases in compensation in excess of the guidelines. Then, of course, the all-powerful administrator would have his power broadened in compensation and dividend cases.
The minister also claimed that significant progress was being made in slowing the rate of inflation. As to that, I can only echo my hon. friend from York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) who quoted the report of the conference board which stated that the recent moderation in the rate of inflation was due almost entirely to a decline in the food component, and that it would be erroneous to give credit to the control measures. Certainly, the Liberal government does nothing to help when it introduces a so-called cutback budget showing estimates 16 per cent higher than those of last year. These proposed amendments do nothing to relieve the plight of the pensioner who relies on dividend income, or to ease the raising of capital so as to encourage investment by Canadians in Canadian enterprise. Nor do they solve the problem of raiding or transfers between companies with the object of circumventing the rules. Still awaited, also, is some relief from the mountain of forms and interminable extra work required to be done by the business community. These are all reflected in passthrough costs, and it is the taxpayer who pays in the end.
Some firms are still trying to understand why they are not entitled to the protection, as they perceive it, which is being given to the larger firms. It is obvious to me that the scheme is never likely to be accepted readily by the Canadian people, principally because it is so confusing to

the community at large and because the government cannot make it appear to work equitably. I suppose we shall be looking for more amendments to the legislation as the days go by.

Mr. Speaker, my words on this occasion will be relatively brief, but I should like to cover a few points that concern me about this bill. My original understanding was that the Anti-Inflation Board rulings would apply to some 1,500 firms. This has now been extended to cover some 20,000 firms. The number of people employed to perform this function appears to me to have been increased by about 2 Vi times the original number. I find this somewhat inconsistent with the original philosophy of the Anti-Inflation Board and I hope that in his concluding remarks the minister will deal a little more fully with this particular point than has been the case up to now.
One favourable feature of the legislation is the expansion of the right of appeal to unions. Originally, the appeal structure was limited to the party that considered itself aggrieved, the government and the party being privy to the ruling. The paying party, the payer of the salary or wages, originally was the only party that could launch an appeal against the ruling of the board. This right has now been extended to the unions, and this is as it should be since a person who receives a salary or wage is as much interested as the person who pays. Wherever possible, it is most undesirable to interfere with freely negotiated agreements as to wages arrived at between employers and employees, but in cases that do exceed the guidelines it is extremely important that both parties to the agreement have the right to appeal the board's ruling to a superior tribunal. I think this is a very good feature of the bill.
Significantly, Mr. Speaker, this change seems to have been brought about as a result of a ruling affecting the Irving enterprises and the paperworkers in New Brunswick. In his concluding remarks, I hope that the minister will have the opportunity of dealing with this particular case. The woods workers of New Brunswick too, are in a very difficult position. Our forests, particularly in the northeastern part of the province, are in a very high state of irreversible decay. When these trees are cut, some go to the sawmill and others go to the pulp and paper factories. The original concept of the sawmills was an extremely good one and flowed from our forest products royal commission study and report. The report recommended, among other things, that we use the best part of the tree for quality products. For example, we use the trunk of the

tree, the best wood, to make finished lumber, furniture or hardwood components, whereas the balance of the tree could be turned into porridge and possibly commercial paper or a more finished form of paper. This recommendation is one that I strongly support. As a result of DREE participation a pilot project sawmill was erected in New Brunswick to perform this very valuable function.
A great deal of difficulty has been encountered with this lumber due to the high degree of decay. One of the major reasons for this decay is that the spruce budworm attacks our forests in New Brunswick and over $5 million of federal money has been allocated to deal with the problem. Indeed, the province has put up even more money than that, as have the industries of the province. So that although we have a three-pronged attack on the budworm, all that our attack on the budworm can do at this point is to control the damage it does. Scientists, particularly in agencies of the federal government, are working on the ultimate solution.
To return to these woodworkers, with this high degree of rot an extensive amount of sorting has to be done in New Brunswick which is not the case with woodsworkers elsewhere. I hope that full weight was given to this fact when the decision affecting the Irving company was taken: Irving is the only firm in New Brunswick that made it a requirement that after the trees are cut, reforestation should take place. They are one of the leaders in North America in this field, and I give them full credit for it. I hope this point was taken into consideration in the wage settlement arrived at between the Irving company and its employees and that it was looked at from a regional point of view.
I should also like to refer to a rumour I have heard from New Brunswick which I hope the minister will be able to shoot down. I understand that in granting the wage increase that was disallowed, the Irving firm, in effect, brought its wage earners up to the national level. I would be very unhappy if I felt that this government has in any way impaired the opportunity of anyone in Atlantic Canada reaching wage parity with Canadians in the central provinces.
Much hard work has been done in this House to reverse the trend whereby not all but some people in Atlantic Canada are paid two-thirds the national wage rate. I would hope this board would not be allowed to operate in such a way as to bring about a freeze in respect of New Brun-swickers, maritimers and the people in Quebec because of the disparity in which they find themselves. The minister partly dealt with this matter in committee. I hope he will have an opportunity to do so again. I would appreciate it if he would deal with it again.
Another thing which concerns me is whether this program can be terminated by resolution of the House. If I read the regulations correctly, the resolution would also have to be dealt with by the other place, as my learned friend to the left refers to it. I should like to reflect on that a little further. Perhaps we might conclude that a limit should be placed on the amount of debate in the other place so that this program could be very quickly brought to an end if that should be the decision of parliament.
Anti-Inflation Act
Another thing we should realize, in dealing with this matter-and perhaps the board should realize it in dealing with applications from New Brunswick-is that there are great problems in that province in respect of transportation. Transportation rates have been increasing in respect of our primary products. This has caused very considerable concern. The province came up with a very dramatic, far-reaching and enlightened program of highway construction over a period of four years. Regrettably, the federal government has not seen fit to join the province in this $400 million undertaking. It has approved some badly needed road construction with regard to arterial highways in northern New Brunswick, but has completely deleted the program for southern New Brunswick.
In answer to my question which appeared on the order paper, it is suggested that no specific request was made for any particular project. However, the whole proposal was before the DREE people and only part of it was approved. I do not know what the Premier of New Brunswick must do in order to ask his federal counterparts to deal with this problem. I know he was here in Ottawa in December, at which time he did everything possible to bring it to the attention of the people concerned. If New Brunswick workers must travel on less favourable roads, or on a less favourable transportation system, then surely wage considerations should involve such concepts. This is in line with what the Irving firm did in dealing most favourably with the matter of wages. This seems to be a move in the direction of what I hoped would be encouragement rather than discouragement, as has been the case in respect of this policy. I am not sure the board has adequate regional representation in order to take into account regional problems.
I shall conclude my remarks by saying I certainly do not expect the minister to deal with all the points I have raised, but I must say he certainly made an effort to deal with all the points I raised previously. If he has an opportunity, I hope he will give some consideration to these points also.

Mr. Speaker, I will not indulge in reiterating what some of my colleagues have said during this debate. They went back to before the last election and indicated how the government brought in a program which it had so vigorously opposed before the 1974 election campaign.
I should like to refer to this in another way. When the government finally structured its anti-inflation program, it was no surprise to me that there was a system of wage and price controls in Canada. I said this to my Liberal opponent during the election campaign. I felt sorry that he had to tell political untruths to the people during the campaign. We both knew that our economy was in trouble and that something would have to happen in tune with what other countries have done to bring the flood and spiral of inflation under control. What I am upset about is that when the government finally decided enough time had expired since the last election campaign, and that it was safe to go to the Canadian people and say, "While this was not a good program in July, it is a good program now," the government also applied, for the first time, this innocuous thing we have heard throughout the debate, that the program is substantially different. In other words, the anti-inflation

March 26, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
program with which the Minister of Finance burdened the people had to be substantially different from the well thought-out plan of the former leader of the opposition.
What did the members of the government do? They sat in the backrooms and went through the Conservative antiinflation program. They must have told themselves, first of all, that they could not have a 90-day freeze because that would look too much like the Conservative program. They decided not to have a time limit of 18 months or 12 months, because that was what the Conservatives discussed during the 1974 election. So they ended up with a program that was substantially different from that worked out and thought out by some people who worked on the problem over a long period. They did not bring in an anti-inflation program that would have worked, a program which indeed did work in the United States and a program that has worked and has helped to bring the economy under control in other parts of the world.
I do not wish to give too much credit to our friends in the fifth estate, but recently a reporter for a local paper said that a government shows its decay never more clearly than when it begins to spend more of its time saving face than fulfilling its mandate. Truer words have never been spoken about this government. This anti-inflation program has been nothing but an effort to save face. It is nothing more than a program that is substantially different to something that might have worked in Canada. At no time did we say that our program was a cure-all or a solution to all the economic problems we face in Canada. We did say, however, that it was a program that was needed to combat the inflationary cycle and bring it under control.
A short while ago the minister asked permission to ask a question of one of my colleagues who spoke about this matter before we recessed for lunch. He asked what the Conservative program would have been. Well, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I can save myself the trouble of responding, if the minister should feel the urge to ask me the question, because I would tell him to ask the former minister of finance who in Toronto recently laid out exactly what he thought the anti-inflation wage and price control program should be like. He said that the open-ended program in effect now could lead to totalitarian government. This is the minister who has just left the cabinet, the former minister of finance. He was also involved in the 1974 election campaign, when he said that the program should have started with a 90-day freeze. I wonder where he got that from, and I wonder why he left the cabinet.
This program is doomed to failure even if the amendments are brought in. When the minister first introduced the program in the House of Commons, and his colleagues spoke on it, great care was taken because it was being said that he would build a monstrous bureaucracy. We were under the same attack in the 1974 election campaign. With regard to the anti-inflation program, we were told that only 200 people in total would administer the program throughout the country and that it would be a kind of self-liquidating program. I invite anyone to travel throughout the country to see how many adjudicators, arbitrators, communicators and instigators are travelling around trying to make this program work, trying to earn the respect of labour and the business community, and trying

to explain the inexplicable; in other words, trying to explain something for which there is no explanation.
My colleagues have spoken about the monstrous forms which small firms have to hire armies of consultants, lawyers and accountants to fulfil the new requirements which the government has placed upon them. What about this business of the jurisdiction of the anti-inflation program? When the program was introduced, my colleagues will recall that the minister said-and I made an issue of this in the House-that basically certain sections of the Income Tax Act would be used by the Anti-Inflation Board in exercising their power to intervene. Generally speaking, anyone who falls under the jurisdiction of the Income Tax Act would fall also under the jurisdiction of the AntiInflation Act. We know that that did not work out the way it was intended, because none of the current operations of the federal government or of the provincial governments- and those are the ones affected by the Income Tax Act and considered different from ordinary departments of the government-is attuned to the anti-inflation program.
The provinces did not fall over themselves to rush to Ottawa and sign the agreements provided for under the act, because first they had to get their own house in order. They wanted to be the first to introduce increased rates for hydro and increased insurance rates such as in British Columbia, which has increased these rates by 120 per cent and 150 per cent in some cases, and all the other costs which make up the cost of living of Canadians. Some provinces found themselves in a pinch with regard to the professional salaries of nurses, teachers, and so on, so they decided it was time to go to the federal minister to sign the program and to refuse to grant the increases which some of these professional groups are demanding.
With a program like this, how can you ask a private sector, the Canadian Labour Congress or the man on the street to practice restraint, to fall in line? These agreements with the provinces have not worked out, and the reason they have not worked out is that the federal government should have shown some restraint. As a matter of fact, we are faced in this House with a 20 per cent increase in federal spending at a time when everybody is being asked to restrain their demands to 10 per cent. On top of that, the government saw fit to shift some of its own responsibilities to the provinces by announcing the phasing out of its participation in certain health programs and the curtailment of some of its contributions to health care over a number of years. Recently, the provinces were faced with the decision of the federal government, reached without any consultation with them, to slow down spending when it comes to policing. The formula is being adjusted, without consultation. The provinces were told they had to accept the greater share in the cost of monitoring the program.
The Unemployment Insurance Act is a perfect example of this. I am referring to the recent adjustments to the Unemployment Insurance Act whereby a qualifying period of six weeks was brought in under the legislation. I challenge any member of the House to show me one working person in our country who could live for six weeks without income. What has been achieved by that change is that the burden to maintain families with no income is now shifted from the federal government to the provincial govern-
March 26, 1976

ments. So why should the provinces be so excited about the anti-inflation program, and why should they act in a different way from the federal government? The provinces had every justification to do what they did through their Crown corporations, to increase hydro rates, the cost of energy, the cost of transportation and all the other essential components in the budget of the average Canadian, particularly those Canadians who can least afford these increases.
When he goes to the bargaining table, the first thing the employer tells the working Canadian is, "We understand you have fallen behind, but you must understand that we are bargaining under some restraints. After all, we want to be responsible Canadians and we do not want to exceed the guidelines that have been set by the federal government." This is the main topic of discussion across the bargaining table today. Unions are charging that no one else is living by the guidelines. Corporations are not following the guidelines, particularly those exporting their goods and who are being paid on international markets.
The minister has announced that their profits, which may be in excess of the guidelines, are allowed under the program. I do not argue with him. I am part owner of a small company which exports all its productive capacity to another part of the world, and I welcome the minister's decision. But I should like to hear from him how he will monitor these excess profits and ensure that they will be funnelled back to the company to be reflected in the increased capacity of the individual plant. It is an exercise in futility. It is impossible to have that kind of transfer of money.
One of my big objections to the program is that it will do nothing in the first year but guarantee us a 10 per cent inflation rate. I can substantiate that argument with the experience we have gained in monitoring the cost of houses and rents in the two major metropolitan centres of Toronto and Vancouver. My colleagues will recall that in British Columbia the socialist government there in 1973 and 1974 had a rent control program: landlords were not allowed to increase rents by more than 10.6 per cent a year. Everyone in the House knows that the cost of housing and rents is the highest in the country in Toronto and Vancouver. The effects of the rent control program in British Columbia were monitored in this way and resulted in rents in Vancouver increasing 3 per cent more in that one year than they did in Toronto. Everyone asked how that was possible, because there was a ceiling on rent and no one was allowed to increase it by more than 10.6 per cent.
The answer is very simple and obvious. Every landlord in the city of Vancouver, whether he wanted to or not-or needed to or not-would have been a damned fool had he not increased his rent by 10.6 per cent, because he did not know what was coming the next year. So every landlord and everyone who rented anything to anyone increased his rent by 10.6 per cent. In the city of Toronto there were some people who did not need an increase that year and they did not operate under those restraints. They knew that if they needed an increase the next year, they could increase rents by 6 per cent, 8 per cent or 15 per cent. The result was a 3 per cent differential.
Anti-Inflation Act
I have operated several small businesses in my business career. If I was in business right now-and there are thousands of small businessmen throughout this country

 every time I would walk through my plant I would look at this and that and make little notes. The Anti-Inflation Board tells me I cannot increase prices more than four times a year, so every three months I would automatically increase my prices. Every day I would look very closely for what I could find to demonstrate to the Anti-Inflation Board a legitimate cost increase as a result of which I could increase my prices. So the effect is this: instead of increasing one's prices once a year or not at all, which was the practice before, one now increases prices four times a year. The effect will be monstrous. Unions will also bargain for the maximum. They will have to, knowing how the anti-inflation program applies to the business sector and the public sector, and knowing how the intrusion of the anti-inflation program into the private enterprise system has affected the economy. Private enterprise will also have to bargain for the maximum in order to protect its skin.
We have not broken the inflationary cycle; we have accelerated the process. Unions will have to try to achieve the maximum because their employers will try to keep them down, and the Anti-Inflation Board will probably roll them back. Recently we have seen settlements in excess of 20 per cent. Unions are shopping all over for these historical relationships. Nobody seems to be able to explain this thing. Some have it, some do not. If you have it, do not fight it. What is an historical relationship? What do you have to catch up to historically? These are some of the questions unions and business people ask themselves, and until some almighty administrator tells them whether they have it or not, nobody will know.
This program does nothing to battle the problems we are facing in our industrial relations. The government is stimulating industrial warfare: the labour movement is more divided today than it ever was as a result of this massive intervention, and the adversary system which exists in labour negotiations is more prevalent today than it was before the program was introduced. We hear voices from every corner and from every sector of our society- and every knowledgeable economist has offered his views on this matter. The C.D. Howe Institute recently published a little booklet which was distributed amongst all my colleagues: it laid out, in no uncertain terms, what the effects of this anti-inflation program would be, even after the amendments are discussed and implemented-if they are implemented as a result of this debate.
As I mentioned before, the former minister of finance has finally broken the silence and entered the public debate, warning the government where the program will lead. This is why we are getting the reaction we are to some of the other legislation that is now before the House. There is an uproar among honest, hard working citizens throughout the country. There is reaction to some of the peace and security legislation, and so on, because people are beginning to think that the great intellect which is within the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has a master plan and that the anti-inflation program might lead us to a destination for which we have not bought our ticket. We are concerned about the recent announcement of the Prime Minister respecting dealing with unions, and his talk about the massive intervention which is required to decontrol

March 26, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
and phase out the anti-inflation program, if indeed that will be possible after a three-year or four-year period.
I hope the former minister of finance will be more vocal and will tell us just how this program came about and why it was necessary for him to leave the cabinet and disassociate himself from the obvious dilemma which was being cooked up in the back room by people who obviously had not given any thought to the problem at hand.
The Prime Minister met with the labour unions just recently, as my colleagues know, and told them that their meeting here-there were only about 15,000 of them marching up and down in front of this building-really would be of no consequence because they would be naive to think that the government would reconsider its program, and that it would be naive for them to think that the government would reconsider the duration of time over which the program should operate. So they went away peacefully and they have embarked upon certain actions.
The Prime Minister has indicated that he is prepared to sit down with labour and talk about the new society and the adjustments which will have to be made in our society before the program can be phased out. We all know about the year-end message of the Prime Minister which caused so much anxiety amongst Liberal backbenchers. They found it necessary to sit down with their leader over a whole weekend and have him explain to them what he meant by this new society and this massive intervention in business and labour and the Prime Minister now says to labour that he is prepared to sit down with them, but with them only. He is not prepared to sit down with them and business people to talk about the the anti-inflation program, about further changes which need to be made, or about the decontrol period; however, he is willing to sit down with labour and talk about how it will be affected by the new society and what kind of intervention into labour he will be planning before he considers this society prepared to live without these controls.
Then I assume he will tell the corporations, chambers of commerce, manufacturers' associations and the people who come to Ottawa to lobby and consult with him, that he will be prepared to carry on this consultation process with them as well, and perhaps he will share with them his views about the new society and how the intervention will affect them.
However, we can rest assured-I know my hon. colleagues will agree with me-that the Prime Minister will never get all these groups into the same room, because that could be dangerous. That would be a departure from his tradition to divide and conquer and to do away with this consultation process where everyone gets into the same room and tries to reach agreement.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
Frankly, the program suffers because the government lacks credibility. Its difficulties began when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced it in his famous message on Friday, October 14, and gave us all great indigestion on Thanksgiving eve. It would not have mattered so much if the government had brought forward a reasoned, reasonable program of wage and price controls. Unfortunately, that was not the case. The government adopted our program. Unfortunately, it ignored its best features and adopted instead some of the worst features of the program we brought forward in the last election campaign. I am under the impression that the present controls program constitutes the sole attack upon inflation. Ignoring action long overdue for curbing inflation, the government has failed to implement concurrent fiscal and monetary policies for slowing down and halting inflation. The controls program, as I say, is the sum and substance of the government's attack on inflation. As the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River has said, this government has reneged on its responsibilities with respect to certain programs, medicare being an example. On the whole, the government has adopted a slapdash approach in its attack on inflation.
Some people question the constitutionality of important parts of the program, and belatedly the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has said that he may seek direction from the Supreme Court. He, too, wants to know if certain aspects of the program, particularly agreements with the provinces, are constitutionally valid. If the Supreme Court finds that parts of the program, agreements with the provinces especially, are not constitutionally valid, there will be chaos piled upon chaos in this country. Various groups in society, teachers included, will make salary demands the like of which we have not seen for a long time. As I say, this government's approach to the whole question has been slapdash. It patches here, fixes there, and introduces an amending bill only weeks after this House passed the original bill. Although the government was thinking of controls before October 14, it had no clear idea where it
March 26, 1976

was going. Now it will take the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada for judicial decision on the constitutionality of the agreements with the provinces.
Controls are disrupting our lives. Let me give a personal example which no doubt could be repeated many times. A couple of weeks ago, late one Sunday night when I returned to my apartment after visiting my constituency I was surprised to find attached to my door a pamphlet on which was printed, so to speak, the modern-day equivalent of Martin Luther's thesis. In so many words, the pamphlet told me that the landlord wanted to apply to the rent review board for a substantial rent increase made necessary by increased costs. I can tell you, at one o'clock in the morning that was a shock to my system.
I discovered, after asking questions, that many landlords in Ottawa-indeed, landlords all over Ontario-are asking for rent increases. Rent increases are to be limited; hence they are asking for the maximum rent allowed. Part of the problem is that the government's control program was without a termination date, and according to all indications, restrictions will be in force for a long time. People were putting pressure on provincial governments to control rents even before the government introduced its antiinflation program. The matter was made worse when the federal government introduced its wage and price control program but without a termination date. Landlords say to themselves, "We must protect our investment and apply for the maximum rent increase or we shall be left out in the cold. We will apply for it and pass on as much as possible the cost of the increase to the unfortunate consumer." I know that in my province of Saskatchewan there is concern because of the pressure placed upon the availability of rental accommodation. More and more owners of apartment buildings are making application under the provincial condominium act to turn existing apartment buildings into condominiums. Rather than renting space within the building, they will be able to sell each apartment.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: Shame!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
It is a shame, for the reason that if this practice continues and is widespread there will be a very great shortage of rental accommodation. People who have the resources will buy accommodation to protect themselves from increases in rent hrought about by pressure being placed upon them by landlords. Unfortunately, with the rent control plan in effect there is a natural discouragement to people investing in building new rental accommodation. We find ourselves now, after a long period which has certainly not been characterized by leadership, in a position in which it has been suggested through various sources that there should be a wage and price control program. Mr. Speaker, this is a sorry reflection upon the administration of the Liberals over the past decade. They have brought us to a position in which our leader recognized, during the election of 1974, that such a policy was essential. The Liberals denied it was called for, yet today, without a mandate from the electorate to do so, they have brought in a hodge-podge program purporting to control wages and prices. This has created a very unjust burden for a great many people in Canada.
I would ask Your Honour to bear in mind that the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), our then leader, said that there should be a 90 day freeze. As has been mentioned before in this House, the man who was then the minister of finance for Canada has since said that if wage and price controls were to be brought in there must be a 90 day freeze. Is this why he left the cabinet, Mr. Speaker? Or did he leave the cabinet because of some of the other ulterior, behavioural patterns existing in cabinet at the time with which he must have been familiar? It must have been one of the two.
We now find ourselves with a program that began by making many exceptions and which-I think this is quite justifiable criticism on the part of the labour sector of our society-has not been effective in controlling prices, and cannot be effective in controlling prices as the program presently operates. The government has created, perhaps intentionally-and that is what alarms me-friction within our society by allowing exceptions to be made to the program, and by exercising no active control over prices other than in cases legislated to the provinces by agree-

ment. As the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) said, the program does control rents.
Was it intended to stir up a furore? Was the plan intended to be criticized by those who said it would not work? Because if that were intentional the government could have devised no better way to engender criticism of the government and doubt among the people of Canada.
Let me give the House an example of how one person feels who has felt the brunt of this program. I want to read to the House a letter addressed to me:
Dear Sir:
I am writing to you to express my disapproval to the present antiinflation program. Being a proud Canadian I would be the first to agree something had to be done to stem the tide of economic disaster that our country is headed for. Wage and price control I am not against, but I am definitely against the present system where our present government freezes the income of the wage earner (not the prices) and segregates one Canadian from the other, because one is from the east and one from the west, when they say the west has always been ahead of the east. Is this democracy? They didn't do this to us when world war II started; when we were mixed up in the forces at that time we all had one common denominator, our love for Canada.
We tradesmen at Irving Pulp and Paper were given a 25 cent increase to adjust our wages to come closer to our western paper workers. We lost that. We fought for our COLA clause. We lost that. We negotiated for N.B. day as most New Brunswickers now enjoy. We lost that. Other things we lost, along with a large per cent of our wages, but most of all we lost our bargaining rights. I love Canada and I love freedom. That is why I am writing you, appalled at the dictatorial tactics taken by Mr. Trudeau and his cabinet.
The really significant thing about that letter, Mr. Speaker, is that the writer, who is prepared to accept wage and price controls, is a union member and a victim of the administration of the Anti-Inflation Board. Yet he is still prepared to accept wage and price control because of the economic situation that he recognizes is Canada's mess of pottage today. It is not that labour is against wage and price control as such; it is against the plan as conceived and administered by the government.
It is incredible that before people can appeal a government decision they must first break the law. This is precisely what happened in the city of Saint John to people who had bargained so long and so well in good faith, and who historically have had such excellent relations with their employer, with a minimum of strikes interrupting the progress of business.
I think one has to recognize the way in which both the company and the union were prepared to face the situation. Both parties, law-abiding groups, agreed that the law had to be broken after a fine had been assessed in order to appeal the decision. How they feel about the situation has been pretty clearly stated in their presentation to the cabinet. For instance, one point they made was that they felt they should remain in the same relative earning position as their fellow workers, the woodlands workers. The agreement signed by the paper workers and the paper mill would have brought the wages of the paper workers up to those of the woodlands workers. An historic relationship had existed between them for years, and historic relationships were to be recognized in Anti-Inflation Board decisions.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion on which I have participated in any debate in respect of the government's anti-inflation program. However, I welcome this opportunity this afternoon to say a few words in this regard.
My memory is very clear concerning the election campaign of June and July of 1974. I remember particularly the impassioned speeches made by my Liberal opponent during the campaign when, on platform after platform, and at candidate forums he equated controls with every aspect that was foreign to Canadian life. He equated freedom, particularly the brand that was to be provided by the Liberal government, with everything that was true and equal to Canadian life. Had he been elected in that campaign and sitting in this House last Thanksgiving Day he would have had to resign the next day because there would have been no possibility of his living with the moves being made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet ministers.
It amazes me still how this program we are debating today could have been set at play at any point without mass resignations from the other side. I will never be able to understand how it could have passed through caucus, through cabinet, and into parliament after the campaign of the summer of 1974. I and millions of other Canadians watched breathlessly as the grab bag of goodies was unloaded across the country. One day there would be reference to a transportation bill, and another day to a housing bill involving billions of dollars. This gave the people a hope for expansion in the future. Unfortunately for the country those promises were taken 6s being true. That assumption has been shattered.
In this debate I should like to pay tribute to my colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), because he saw the situation as it was developing. He sounded a warning, well in advance of Thanksgiving Day, because he knew what was coming. The hon. member is not in the House and I know he is too modest to regard himself as even a minor prophet, but I am sure his judgment as to what was coming out of government offices was solidly on the line.
It was interesting this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) use the word "terminated". During his address it occurred to me that the program of the government has been "Turner-rat-

ed" in the last week. The former minister of finance rated it a solid zero and indicated what should have been done.
It might be some solace to the official opposition, and certainly to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) to know that what they proposed was what the former minister of finance sees now as what should have been, and was, the only possible road to follow in entering this delicate and important question of controls. That must have been quite a cabinet meeting at which he told his colleagues the only way they could go was to follow the plan suggested by the leader of the opposition. Obviously that was not possible for the government opposite, so that minister of finance resigned and is no longer in this House. Instead of accepting what was not palatable to the Liberals, the government embarked upon a policy of wage and price controls which must by its very nature tighten down, tighten down, and tighten down.
The possibility of easing up becomes more remote every day. The inequities that have been introduced, which this bill attempts in some way to overcome, grow larger and larger day by day. There have been some statements in the press suggesting that the rate of inflation has slowed and that the scheme is working. I suggest seriously that those figures are illusory, and that if there has been any slowing down it has been at the expense of the farmers who receive lower prices for their produce, and at the expense of the companies that are going out of business at fire sale prices across this country because of the program put in place by the government, and because there are very few areas of the Canadian economy that are allowed to fluctuate freely any longer. There will be an even lower percentage of the economy that will be able to fluctuate in any way. The program that is before us will not assist very much in that regard.
I would like to bring to the attention of the minister one example of the kind of frustrations that have been brought to my notice. I have here an invoice from a hospital in my constituency. On January 19, 1976, it had an invoice for a shipment of Macbick flasks, 3,000 ml. 12 at $87.90. On February 19, 1976, it had an invoice for Macbick flasks, 3,000 ml. 12 at $182. It is at that point that it raised the matter with the Anti-Inflation Review Board. The reply was that the company employed fewer than 500 people and therefore does not come under the guidelines of the AntiInflation Board, so nothing can be done about this.
One hopes that possibly what we are doing under Bill C-89 will provide the Anti-Inflation Review Board with an opportunity to bring some equity here because this is the missing element in the approach taken by the government. I am not an economist, but when the program was announced I heard it would be restricted to those corporations that employ 500 employees or more and it struck me then that there was not a shred of hope that the program could succeed on that basis. I believed that it would only be a matter of time until we were presented with the bill that is before us today because nothing as inequitable as that can hope to succeed.
But the government in all its efforts has endeavoured to make the suggestion that it was really going after big business, even though it has been in the hands of big
Anti-Inflation Act
business for a long time. There was a hope in the announcement that some popularity could be bought at the expense of the larger corporations, but in these days of automation a great deal of manufacturing can be done with far fewer than 500 employees.
There was a false hope that the government was really going to take some firm action and do something about inflation. We know that initially the response across the country was good, and that in the year during which the former minister of finance endeavoured to persuade the various sectors of the Canadian economy to get together and form a consensus, public opinion began to harden on the whole question, and there was a growing realization that the program presented by the official opposition would have been the wiser choice in 1974. It is regrettable that the prime minister of this country was not the hon. member for Halifax, as he should have been.
I am concerned about the decision recently taken by the representatives of labour who were consulted during that search for consensus. I wonder if the former minister of finance had set up an all encompassing board-I do not know what power it would have had because of course it would not have had any power until some legislation had been presented to parliament-a board where all the sectors of the economy met and talked together, whether the representatives of labour would have taken the chair that was reserved for them at such a board.
I regret the intransigence and the separation of that very important part of the Canadian economy from various boards, because certainly if the scheme which has been presented to us-with all its errors and shortcomings, its inequities and confusions, with a board that does not know what it is doing and is not likely to know for many months ahead, with the emphasis on wage controls and the apparent inability to do anything about prices-is to be successful, it will require the co-operation of every sector of the Canadian economy. Only then can the inflation rate in Canada be slowed down.
I know how many institutions in this land, which are absolutely vital to the country, are bedeviled at present by inflation. All kinds of voluntary and church organizations, schools and hospitals, almost every institution that holds together the fabric of this country, are threatened now as they never have been since the great depression of the 1930's.
It is important that an equitable incomes policy be arrived at, but I do not see any hope that this method of approaching case by case individually will ever produce anything like a recognizable policy, and even as the cases are decided one after another a feeling will be left that justice has not been done. The situation will grow darker rather than lighter even if we pass Bill C-89.
