Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the courtesy of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway) in cutting his remarks short so I might say just a word in this important debate.
It is not astonishing that the matter is back before the House because the need for an amendment asking for an extension of the coverage of this operation was quite clear from the time the government first brought in controls because it brought them in in an incorrect fashion. Everyone said that an incomes policy should cover everyone. It should be universal, fair, and should have started with a 90-day freeze. We now have the statement of a former minister who, presumably, was responsible for some of this program, saying in retrospect that that is the way it should have been started. The fact that it did not happen that way means we are back with the kind of amendment we are talking about today. I expect that as time goes by we will find there will be further amendments as the government finds that the way in which it has approached this program is not working.
A couple of days ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), speaking in this debate, seemed to suggest that controls will be instrumental in curbing rising expectations and that they are capable of solving this country's inflationary difficulties. I say to him, as many others have said-and this should be repeated constantly-that controls will not solve inflation. They cause distortions in the economy and inequities, and we are reaping the results today of some of those inequities in terms of the response of the labour movement of this country to the way in which the controls program has been operating.
If the government had followed the advice of the opposition, and of most economists who have spoken on the subject, and adopted an across-the-board freeze, many of the problems we are seeing at present would have been avoided. I rather hoped, when the present Minister of Finance was appointed, to see an improvement in the country's economic policies. I thought no one could be as bad as the previous minister of finance. However, having heard the present minister speak, and read his speeches, it seems to me that we are not yet out of the woods.
I find it absolutely astonishing that the Minister of Finance should have spent considerable time accusing the opposition of lacking consistency in its approach to the controls program. Does the government not realize that controls, like any other economic policy, must be designed to solve a specific problem? In some circumstances controls are not proper and correct; in some circumstances they are. The position of the Minister of Finance that, regardless of economic circumstances, we shall face controls for another one and a half or two years, is fraught with difficulty.
I am also worried because the minister is still talking about a trace-off between inflation and unemployment. Surely if one thing has become clear in the last two or three years in the developed countries of the world it is this: the trade-off between unemployment and inflation does not exist within reasonable limits.
We know that Canada's economic policies have been bad. Nobody can be proud of a no-growth year, double digit inflation-it is getting slightly better now-and 7 per cent

unemployment. When you say that there is less inflation in the United States and hear the minister respond, "Yes, but their unemployment rate is up," you know the Government of Canada still believes in the old trade-off principle, a principle rejected all over the world because it is not valid.
It was also startling to hear the Minister of Finance say that we should cavalierly adopt an expansionary policy and not worry about deficits. If there is one thing that is certain and on which there is almost total agreement, it is that the cause of inflation in western industrialized democracies is the enormous deficits governments have continued to run. The Minister of Finance seems to suggest that when members of my party, and economists, say that our long term goal should be a balanced budget, without which there will be no recovery, our approach is reacti-nary. Unless the government realizes that it must balance expenditures against revenues, we are in for a lot of inflation for a long time.
We have 50 per cent more inflation than the United States because we have not introduced the right monetary policies and have done nothing about our deficit. That is why we suffer from our present inflation. The view that we shall solve the country's inflation with this ill-conceived, poorly run incomes policy, and not with the proper fiscal and monetary policies, is most discouraging.
In his last speech the minister quoted the Governor of the Bank of Canada. That governor came before the parliamentary committee in the spring of 1973 saying that we do not need any sort of incomes policy to restrain our economy. That same governor was in favour of an expansionary policy, when everybody said we needed a policy of contraction. That same Governor of the Bank of Canada today is talking about a roughly 10 per cent expansion in our money supply, when the United States is talking about a 2 per cent expansion of its money supply. It is regrettable that the Minister of Finance should depend at this time on advice of that sort.
It is apparent that the economic outlook for Canada in the next year or so is dismal because the government is again saying, as it always has said, that what happens here depends on what happens in other countries.
As we approach four o'clock let me say this: the remarks of the Minister of Finance made the day before yesterday reveal that there is no change in the way the Government of Canada is approaching economic policy, no change in its understanding of the fundamental causes of inflation in the country. There is no evidence that it recognizes that high interest rates are no solution to inflation. We are still clinging to the old trade-off idea, to the theory that you can trade off inflation against unemployment. Therefore the economic prospects of the country in the immediate future are dim indeed-unless we can reduce our deficits, borrow less through the public treasury and introduce sound fiscal policy. Otherwise inflation will continue. We may be pleased at the recent drop in inflation rates, caused by what happened recently in the agricultural food industry, but the point is that it was an aberration. Statistics show that we shall face a difficult time for the balance of the fiscal year.
Many hon. members were discouraged last Thursday when they heard the Minister of Finance speak on this bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH EMERGENCY TELEPHONE NUMBER
speechtext:
that Bill C-252, to establish a universal emergency telephone number, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the National Transportation Act by adding immediately after Section 22(1) (i) the following:
(j) provide for the establishment by all Canadian telephone companies of a universal emergency reporting telephone number.
My purpose for proceeding with Bill C-252 this afternoon is not so much in the expectation that the bill will be passed, a rare occurrence in this House for legislation initiated by private members, but rather in the hope that hon. members will see fit to allow the subject matter of the bill to proceed to committee for detailed study and discussion.
Such discussion, I believe, would serve useful purpose in arousing public interest at the local community and municipal level, which is virtually a prerequisite if a universal

Emergency Telephone Number
emergency telephone number system is to be successful. Indeed this was the goal of the former member for Surrey-White Rock, Barry Mather, who for many years introduced the same type of bill we are debating today. He was known as a member who introduced legislation not so much in the expectation that it would be adopted, but as a prod to the appropriate officials through debate in the House of Commons to move more quickly. On the subject of a universal emergency telephone number, more prodding is needed and, in this regard, I am pleased to take up where the former member left off.
The establishment of a single emergency number through which people can summon police, fire or ambulance help in any city, not only in Canada but in all of North America, and progress in the United States has been very impressive, would be a very important step in the field of public safety. The idea is not new.
An article in the New York Times of Saturday, January 13, 1968, by David Burnham, entitled "U.S. Code Planned for Phoning Help" reads in part as follows:
A plan to establish a national emergency telephone number-911- with which police, fire and ambulance services could be summoned from any telephone in the United States was announced yesterday by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company.
Under the plan, a person needing emergency help would dial 911. His call would be switched to a unified dispatching office established in each community by the police, fire and other emergency services, such as hospitals, and appropriate help would be sent.
The establishment of such a number was recommended last year by the President's Crime Commission.
At least one other country, Britain, already has a simple three-digit number-999-with which to summon emergency help.
Almost since its inception, the telephone has been the primary means for reporting an emergency. For years, people have been either dialing the number of a required safety agency or going through an operator for help. Of course, such methods have had inherent disadvantages.
In an emergency, dialing "zero" for the operator or finding the number of a particular agency involves several steps. A call to a telephone company operator requires a second call by the operator to an emergency agency, and this involves time. Fluctuations in the volume of traffic handled by operators sometimes can delay the immediate response to a call. Also, unless one has a keen memory or a handy reference, there is an unavoidable delay in finding the number for an agency.
To anyone who has required emergency assistance, the number of minor problems and nuisances which can make the situation very agonizing are well known. Perhaps just finding a telephone book can be difficult. Often attempting to pick out which police or fire number should be used, in a list of many, requires an in-depth knowledge of municipal boundaries, something many long time residents do not have, let alone visitors. Of course, there is the problem of the pay phone, difficult enough when the person trying to call first had to find a ten cent coin, doubly so now when you need two such coins. Finally, there are the numbers themselves each with a different mind-cracking combination of seven digits, almost guaranteeing that nobody will be able to remember them when they need them most.
I believe the value of one emergency telephone number is obvious. The existence of a single emergency telephone number makes it quicker and easier for anyone to acquire

emergency assistance. The three digit code "911" was chosen because it is a brief and easily remembered number, and because it is compatible with the long range numbering plans and switching configurations of the telephone companies. It has now been reserved as a universal emergency number so that there will be one standard North American emergency service code.
The 911 number is designed to be used, at no charge to the calling party, for direct reporting of emergencies to an answering bureau serving a given area. The answering bureau is staffed and controlled by the major emergency agencies in the community-fire, police, and ambulance services.
The 911 service provides for a faster response to time. The centralized answering bureau where 911 calls are handled, is staffed by specialized personnel who know how to react. Priority calls can be identified and the proper agency sent out on call. An additional and often overlooked benefit is that by co-ordinating all emergency services in the one bureau a community can collect data and analyse the effectiveness of its emergency services and take immediate steps to correct any deficiencies.
The successful implementation of the single emergency telephone number systems has produced a growing awareness of 911 by many communities in North America. I mentioned the great progress which has been made in this regard south of the border. There are now more than 900 "911" systems operating in the United States, ranging in size from 2,000 to 8,000,000 telephones and estimated to be serving more than 30,000,000 people in all.
As for Canada, progress has been steady if not so noticeable. In 1959 Winnipeg became the first North American city with a three-digit emergency reporting system when it cut over to 999. Brandon has a similar service also utilizing the 999 code. Both of these communities have plans under way to convert to 911. Now there are eight operational 911 systems in the communities of Calgary, Edmonton, Lethbridge and Red Deer in Alberta; London and Kitchener-Waterloo, Ontario; Fredericton, New Brunswick, and St. John's, Newfoundland.
I do not feel that a single emergency telephone number system is the be-all and end-all in the field of public safety. It is only one part, and there are a number of problems which still must be resolved. Perhaps the most important of these problems relates to municipal responsibility.
The concept of 911 is a new idea for most local governments. For the first time, the total emergency resources of a community must be coordinated into a total communications network. This is not achieved by simply changing over to a new telephone number. When a municipality considers 911 it must evaluate the existing procedures and systems for handling emergency calls and be prepared to tackle two basic problems.
First, jurisdictional boundaries of emergency agencies seldom coincide with either telephone exchange boundaries or municipal boundaries, but to avoid confusion agencies must be prepared to serve all those within an individual exchange, or in exchanges having local calling with a core exchange where they may not have jurisdiction. Second, all three major emergency services should be
March 26, 1976

included-police, fire, ambulance. Sometimes individual agencies are reluctant to change their autonomous status because agency administrators may consider command and control of their field resources as a process too important to be shared or delegated to another agency. But regardless of individual agency reluctance to cooperate, an agreement has to be reached at the local level on the establishment of a common answering arrangement.
Free emergency calling and 911 are naturally associated since both provide the public with improved telephone service in time of emergency. The 911 system in London, Ontario, has 73 yellow call boxes located strategically around the city. The call box caller picks up the receiver and gets the answering bureau immediately. No dialing is necessary.
Bell Canada is converting coin telephones across Quebec and Ontario to allow free emergency calling. "Dial-tone first" for coin telephones will enable the user to have access to the operator without a coin in case of an emergency.
In a community offering 911 service the calling party will be able to dial 911 without the deposit when "dial-tone first" is provided. The time-saving advantage is obvious; it will make every public pay telephone a signal box.
Technical innovations and the concentration of sophisticated telephone equipment can greatly enhance emergency services. Techniques are available on order like, "call-hold-and-trace" which holds up the line, the 911 caller uses; the line is frozen and there is a "ring-back" which allows the emergency bureau to ring back a caller. With these features, false alarms and errors can be virtually eliminated thereby increasing public confidence and respect.
I know some will argue that because of jurisdictional and technical problems the subject matter of this bill would best be left with a particular department which has the appropriate expertise to study this subject, rather than to a committee of the House composed of laymen. However, I believe this is an important public matter, one in which the public should have some input. All too often services and programs are structured and designed behind closed doors, and the intended beneficiaries have no say until the services or programs are operational.
There are a number of questions, such as the role of the telephone company and the role of the federal government in the implementation of a universal emergency telephone number, which a committee of the House could and should look into. It may be suggested that this legislation should more properly be an amendment to the Railway Act. However, regardless of this argument the subject matter could still be sent to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
I therefore urge hon. members to allow the subject matter of the bill to proceed to committee.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join with other members in commending the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) on bringing the question of the adoption across Canada of a universal telephone number before the House. I believe it was Bell Canada that in 1968 took the initiative and chosea number to be set aside to serve the whole of North America for emergency use only, the number 911. The value of such a number is obvious. In an emergency people sometimes have difficulty finding the proper number to call. The idea of a central switchboard that would direct calls to the police, firefighting services, drug intervention centres, and poison control centres is a very good one.
Any legislation that we would pass would primarily apply to Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia in view of the jurisdiction we have over the principal telephone systems in those three provinces. Naturally legislation would have to be passed relating to other provinces that have their own telephone systems. I understand that most telephone companies in Canada are co-operating completely in establishing such a system. For example, Bell has new equipment in place to accommodate this single number emergency call.
There is one area in my riding where I hope within the next 12 months new equipment will be put in place to handle not only emergency calls but regular telephone calls. I refer to the Silver Water exchange at the west end of Manitoulin Island where, when equipment is out of service, a person has to drive 25 or 30 miles to re-establish contact, let alone call someone such as a doctor in cases of emergency. I am glad to know that Bell Canada is co-operating, and I hope they will continue to co-operate to the extent of establishing good, workable equipment in all areas, but especially in those rural areas of Canada that still lack proper telephone service.
I understand there is a problem with the bill as presently framed in that it should be an amendment to the Railway Act rather than the National Transportation Act. At the hon. member's suggestion perhaps the subject matter of the bill could be sent to committee rather than the bill itself, if it be the case that the provisions of the National Transportation Act are inappropriate.
To make adoption of this number successful the co-operation of the municipalities and regional governments would be required. It is not merely a case of passing federal legislation approving adoption of this number; there would have to be co-operation with the various municipal agencies such as fire departments, police, drug and poison control centres, and so on. However, any leadership that we would give at the federal level would surely only expedite matters.
I understand that the city of Vancouver has already ordered equipment to handle this universal emergency number, and installation of such equipment is also under consideration in the Cranbrook area. In Alberta, Calgary, Edmonton and Red Deer already have this kind of service under consideration. There are no cities in Saskatchewan that have this service available, but the Saskatchewan telephone system is prepared to offer the service if the

municipalities will make a commitment. Negotiations were under way to serve Regina and Saskatoon in 1973.
The hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore mentioned that in Winnipeg and Brandon this emergency service is available. In the province of Ontario it has been available in London and Kitchener, covering the services of the fire department, police, poison control centre, ambulance dispatch and so on. So some progress is being made, and any leadership given at the federal level would only speed the process across the country. It would also clear away any additional legislative red tape that might be holding things up. I conclude with those few comments. The hon. member has my support in bringing the matter before parliament so that it can be fully aired.

Unless we can be assured through the means of the Procedure and Organization Committee that this type of destruction of a good idea is stopped and an end is put to the abuse of the proceedings of this House in this way, I suspect at least in my own case this will be one of the last times I will ever again contribute to the disposal of a private members' bill by talking it out or even using up the available time.
I want to point out for the benefit of hon. members, who may have some interest in how we deal with this system, precisely what happens. Every session something like 150 or 200 private members' bills are put down by members. About 50 of these are drawn out of a barrel in the Clerk's office. Those 50 bills are put forward in the order drawn and are brought forward for first reading. Of the 50 I do not recall the actual number but I would doubt that more than three or four ever reach committee. Right from the start no distinction is made between bills that are improperly drawn and perfectly good bills.
